specPoints.text: describe these experimental techniques for the separation of mixtures: simple distillation, fractional distillation, filtration, crystallisation, paper chromatography
practical: investigate paper chromatography using inks/food colourings

primer.text: Separation Techniques introduced paper chromatography as a way of splitting an ink into its dyes. This practical turns that idea into a full procedure: setting up the paper, spotting samples, running the solvent, and comparing Rf values so an unknown mixture of colourings can be named. Revisit the chromatography part of Separation Techniques first if the setup still feels new.

lessons.title: Apparatus and Method
lessons.opening: This practical separates the dyes in four known food colourings and an unknown mixture using paper chromatography. Capillary tubes place tiny spots on a pencil start line, water climbs the paper, and each dye travels its own distance. Careful setup matters: every distance you measure later depends on how cleanly the run was carried out.
keyPoints: A pencil start line is drawn 2 cm from the bottom edge of the chromatography paper.
Each colouring gets its own capillary tube, so one sample cannot contaminate another.
Spots are kept no bigger than 2-3 mm so the dyes can pull apart cleanly.
Water goes in to 1 cm or less, keeping the solvent below the pencil line.
The run is left undisturbed until the solvent has climbed at least three quarters of the paper.
A solvent front line is drawn at the wet edge before any distances are measured in mm.

low.restatement: Draw a pencil line 2 cm up the paper, spot every colouring on it with its own tube, stand the paper in 1 cm of water so nothing dissolves too early, and let the solvent climb three quarters of the way before marking the wet edge.
low.analogy: It is a race with strict starting rules: every dye begins together on the same grid line, in its own lane, and nobody moves the finish tape until most of the track is covered.
low.examPointer: Method marks reward order and reasons - pencil first, small spots, shallow solvent, then measure from the start line to the centre of each spot.

medium.restatement: A pencil start line 2 cm from the bottom carries spots of colourings A to D and the unknown U, each placed with a fresh capillary tube and kept within 2-3 mm. The paper stands in water no deeper than 1 cm, clipped to a wooden spill, and the solvent climbs undisturbed until it is at least three quarters of the way up before the wet edge is marked.
medium.analogy: Treat the start line as a race grid and the solvent front as the finish judge: the race is only fair if every runner starts on the grid, stays in lane, and the clock stops at a marked line.
medium.examPointer: For each step, give the reason as well as the action - pencil so the line cannot run, small spots so dyes stay distinct, shallow water so samples begin above the solvent.

check.stem: How far from the bottom of the paper does the pencil start line go?

options.text: 2 cm from the bottom edge
options.explanation: The line sits 2 cm up so the paper below can dip into the solvent without the samples touching it.

options.text: 2 cm from the top edge
options.explanation: The start line is at the bottom; the solvent climbs from it toward the top.
options.misconception: start line placed at the solvent end

options.text: Anywhere on the paper, as long as it is straight
options.explanation: Placement is fixed 2 cm from the bottom; a line elsewhere puts samples in or above the solvent.
options.misconception: measuring position treated as optional

options.text: On the dry upper half, above the water
options.explanation: That confuses the start line with the solvent front, which is only drawn after the run.
options.misconception: start line confused with solvent front

check.stem: Why must each food colouring be spotted with a different capillary tube?

options.text: A used tube would carry traces of the previous dye into the next sample
options.explanation: Cross-contamination would plant foreign spots on the chromatogram and fake a match.

options.text: The tubes soften when reused, so spots would be too large
options.explanation: Tube softness is not the issue; the risk is dye traces, not tube shape.
options.misconception: material wear blamed instead of contamination

options.text: Five tubes are supplied, so all five must be used
options.explanation: The count of tubes is beside the point; each sample needs its own clean tube.
options.misconception: procedural compliance mistaken for the reason

options.text: Different tubes hold different volumes of solvent
options.explanation: Spot size is controlled by how the tube is used, and the concern is mixing samples, not volume.
options.misconception: solvent volume confused with sample purity

check.stem: What is the largest diameter a sample spot may have?

options.text: 2-3 mm, so the separated dyes stay distinct
options.explanation: Tiny, concentrated spots separate into distinct marks that are easy to measure.

options.text: 5 mm, which keeps the pencil line safe
options.explanation: The limit is 2-3 mm and it guards spot separation, not the line.
options.misconception: invented limit attached to the wrong risk

options.text: 1 cm, which keeps the solvent from escaping
options.explanation: Solvent loss is controlled by a lid on the beaker, not by spot size.
options.misconception: evaporation control confused with spot size

options.text: There is no limit; bigger spots give stronger colour
options.explanation: Oversized spots smear and merge, which spoils the measurements.
options.misconception: more sample assumed to mean better data

check.stem: How deep should the water be poured into the beaker?

options.text: No more than 1 cm, so the start line stays above the solvent
options.explanation: Samples must start above the solvent, or they dissolve straight into it instead of climbing.

options.text: About half the beaker, so the paper gets plenty of solvent
options.explanation: Deep solvent would cover the start line and end the run before it begins.
options.misconception: more solvent assumed to mean a better run

options.text: Exactly level with the pencil line
options.explanation: Level with the line means the samples sit in the solvent, which dissolves them away.
options.misconception: touching the line treated as safe

options.text: The depth does not matter as long as spots are small
options.explanation: Depth is the one factor that decides whether samples start above or below the solvent.
options.misconception: spot size mistaken for solvent control

check.stem: When should the paper be lifted out of the beaker?

options.text: After the solvent has travelled at least three quarters of the way up
options.explanation: That gives the dyes room to separate while leaving the front distance measurable.

options.text: As soon as the spots start to move
options.explanation: Lifting that early stops the run before the dyes have spread apart.
options.misconception: first movement mistaken for completion

options.text: When the solvent reaches the very top of the paper
options.explanation: By then the front has run off, and its travel distance can no longer be measured.
options.misconception: maximum run assumed to be best

options.text: After exactly five minutes, whatever the solvent has done
options.explanation: The endpoint is set by how far the solvent front has climbed, not by the clock.
options.misconception: fixed time mistaken for the endpoint

check.stem: State what must be drawn on the paper before any distances are measured.
check.modelAnswer: A solvent front line, drawn at the wet edge (distances are then measured in mm).

check.stem: State the two preparations made before the solvent is poured in.
check.modelAnswer: A pencil start line is drawn 2 cm from the bottom edge of the paper, and each colouring is spotted with its own capillary tube in spots no bigger than 2-3 mm.

check.stem: Explain why sharing one capillary tube between two colourings would spoil the results.
check.modelAnswer: Because each colouring gets its own capillary tube so one sample cannot contaminate another — a shared tube would mix the samples, and the spots would no longer be each dye's own.

check.stem: After an hour a student's solvent front has climbed only halfway up the paper. State what they should do, and why.
check.modelAnswer: Keep the run going — leave it undisturbed until the solvent has climbed at least three quarters of the paper (lifting it before the front reaches the top).

lessons.title: Common Errors and Results
lessons.opening: Most lost marks in this practical come from five avoidable slips: an ink start line, oversized spots, solvent above the line, letting the front run off the paper, and leaving the beaker open. Each has a simple fix, and the results table turns a clean run into Rf values. When the unknown's Rf matches a known colouring, that dye is named.
keyPoints: Ink start lines dissolve and run with the solvent, so every line and label is pencil.
Oversized spots smear and merge, making the Rf value hard to measure accurately.
Solvent above the start line dissolves the samples away, so no dye ever climbs the paper.
A lid on the beaker keeps a solvent vapour atmosphere and stops the run slowing down.
The paper comes out before the solvent front reaches the top, or Rf cannot be calculated.
Matching Rf values mean the unknown holds that same dye, backed up by a visual check.

low.restatement: Five slips ruin the run: ink lines that dissolve, spots too big, solvent over the start line, a front that runs off the top, and an open beaker. Each has a one-step fix, and a clean run gives Rf values that name the unknown's dyes.
low.analogy: Think of the five errors as five ways to spoil a race: a moving start line, runners too wide for their lanes, a grid underwater, a finish past the stadium, and no lid on the clock.
low.examPointer: Error questions ask for cause and fix in one line - name the slip, then state the pencil, small-spot, shallow-solvent, early-lift or lid remedy.

medium.restatement: Ink start lines add their own travelling dyes, oversized spots blur into one another, solvent above the line dissolves the samples before they can climb, an uncovered beaker lets vapour escape and slows the run, and a front that reaches the very top leaves its distance unmeasurable. A clean run fills the results table, and matching Rf values between the unknown and a known colouring identify that dye.
medium.analogy: A covered beaker is like a covered pan: the steam stays in, the process stays steady, and nothing escapes to spoil what you are watching.
medium.examPointer: Rf comparison questions want the logic stated: equal heights and equal Rf values point to the same substance, while a single match proves presence, not purity of the whole unknown.

check.stem: A student draws the start line with ballpoint ink. What happens to the chromatogram?

options.text: The ink's own dyes climb the paper and interfere with the dye spots
options.explanation: Ink is a dye mixture, so it produces extra marks that make the result hard to read.

options.text: Nothing, because ink and pencil mark the paper the same way
options.explanation: Pencil is insoluble; ink dyes dissolve and travel, so the two are not equivalent.
options.misconception: writing tools assumed interchangeable

options.text: The paper dissolves where the ink sits
options.explanation: Paper stays intact; it is the ink that moves, not the paper that breaks down.
options.misconception: solvent damage blamed on the paper

options.text: The sample spots become larger than 2-3 mm
options.explanation: Spot size was fixed when sampling; the ink adds stray marks instead.
options.misconception: two separate errors merged into one

check.stem: Spots were made about 5 mm across. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Neighbouring dyes merge or smear, so distances cannot be measured cleanly
options.explanation: Oversized spots spread into each other and blur the positions of their centres.

options.text: The dyes separate faster because more sample is moving
options.explanation: Extra sample does not speed the solvent; it widens the marks and muddies them.
options.misconception: more sample assumed to speed the run

options.text: The start line dissolves because bigger spots hold more water
options.explanation: The line's safety depends on being drawn in pencil, not on spot diameter.
options.misconception: unrelated cause attached to spot size

options.text: The Rf values come out above 1
options.explanation: Spot size cannot push a spot past the solvent front, so Rf stays below 1.
options.misconception: measurement error blamed on the ratio bound

check.stem: The water was poured to 3 cm, well above the pencil line. What follows?

options.text: The samples dissolve straight into the solvent and no separation happens
options.explanation: Samples must start above the liquid; underwater, they never climb the paper at all.

options.text: The run works normally but takes longer
options.explanation: Submerged samples never begin a climb; time is not the issue.
options.misconception: submersion mistaken for a slow start

options.text: The spots travel further and give bigger Rf values
options.explanation: There is no travel at all, so there is nothing to measure.
options.misconception: distance inflated by extra solvent

options.text: Only the unknown mixture U is affected
options.explanation: Every sample on the line is underwater and every one is lost.
options.misconception: error confined to one sample

check.stem: Why does a watch glass lid on the beaker improve the run?

options.text: It keeps solvent vapour in, so the paper does not dry out and slow the climb
options.explanation: A saturated atmosphere stops solvent leaving the wet paper, keeping the run steady.

options.text: It stops the solvent spilling if the beaker is knocked
options.explanation: Spill protection is incidental; the lid's job is controlling vapour.
options.misconception: safety role invented for the lid

options.text: It raises the temperature so dyes move faster
options.explanation: The lid does not heat anything; it fills the air above with solvent vapour.
options.misconception: heating effect assumed

options.text: It keeps the dyes from evaporating off the paper
options.explanation: Dyes are not volatile; what escapes is solvent from the paper's surface.
options.misconception: dye loss confused with solvent loss

check.stem: Spot U lands level with colouring B, and their Rf values match. What is concluded?

options.text: The unknown mixture contains dye B
options.explanation: Same height and same Rf identify the same substance, and the visual comparison agrees.

options.text: U is pure dye B and nothing else
options.explanation: One matching spot shows B is present; other spots in U would mean more components.
options.misconception: one match taken as the whole composition

options.text: Colouring B must be a mixture of four dyes
options.explanation: B is a known single colouring; it is U whose composition is being probed.
options.misconception: direction of identification reversed

options.text: The result is void because U moved the same distance as B
options.explanation: Matching travel is exactly the evidence the practical is designed to produce.
options.misconception: agreement mistaken for a fault

check.stem: State what happens to ink start lines in the solvent, and what is used instead.
check.modelAnswer: Ink start lines dissolve and run with the solvent, so every line and label is drawn in pencil.

check.stem: State the timing rule for lifting the paper out of the beaker.
check.modelAnswer: The paper comes out before the solvent front reaches the top, or Rf cannot be calculated.

check.stem: Explain why solvent poured above the start line spoils the chromatogram.
check.modelAnswer: Because solvent above the start line dissolves the samples away into the pool of solvent, so no dye ever climbs the paper.

check.stem: Spot U matches colouring B's Rf exactly, but U also shows a second spot that matches nothing in the table. State what U contains.
check.modelAnswer: U contains dye B plus at least one other dye — matching Rf values mean the unknown holds that same dye (backed up by a visual check), and the extra unmatched spot is another component, so U is a mixture.

glossary.definition: Taking a mixture apart into its components by physical means.
The absorbent paper on which the dyes are spotted and separated.
The pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of the paper where all samples are spotted.
A fine glass tube used to place one tiny spot of sample on the start line.
The furthest edge reached by the wet solvent, marked with a pencil line at the wet edge.
The distance moved by a spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent.
Solvent turning to vapour from the wet paper; slowed by a lid on the beaker.

workedExample.prompt: In the paper chromatography practical, the solvent front travels 72 mm from the start line. The blue spot of known colouring B travels 54 mm, and one spot of the unknown mixture U also travels 54 mm, landing level with B. a) Calculate the Rf value of spot U. b) What does the comparison allow you to conclude? c) Explain why the start line is drawn in pencil rather than ink.
steps: a) Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent, so Rf = 54 / 72 = 0.75.
b) Spot U travels the same distance and shares colouring B's Rf value, so the unknown contains the blue dye of colouring B (backed up by the visual match).
c) Pencil marks are insoluble, so the start line stays put; an ink line would dissolve and travel up the paper, adding its own dyes to the chromatogram.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Rf = 0.75. b) The unknown contains colouring B's blue dye. c) Pencil is insoluble and does not run, unlike ink.
